title: Anywhere
synopsis: When teleportation makes locked doors obsolete, design a refuge that balances privacy with accessibility.

intrusion.text: Teleportation made every locked door obsolete. One morning a stranger appears beside your wardrobe, holding a birthday cake and apologizing for landing in the wrong bedroom. By nightfall, the birthday child has seen their parents frightened for the first time. Your city is full of people asking not only who can picture their homes, but who gets to feel safe inside them.

choices.text: Use your work as an architect to make rooms difficult to picture
Help the police investigate a murder in a supposedly private house

studio.text: You design a room with crooked walls, shifting panels, and light that changes how familiar corners look. It works: visitors who have never been there cannot picture a safe arrival. Then your client asks you to make the place accessible to their child, who is afraid of getting lost. A refuge can become another kind of trap.

choices.text: Redesign it for easy navigation, even if it is easier to picture
Keep the layout private and teach the family its landmarks

crime.text: The victim's business partner says he never entered the house. A school photo online shows the room's crooked wall, yellow chair, and blue rug. The picture might have taught the killer the way in, but a likeness is not proof of who used it.

choices.text: Preserve the image trail and demand a careful investigation
Warn every family whose home appears in public photographs

text.value: The child helps you replace the shifting panels with a bright, continuous route they can navigate alone. The room is easier to picture now, but nobody in the family has to ask permission to find the kitchen. You chose a refuge the child could inhabit, not merely one that could hide.

You teach the family the landmarks, and the child memorizes them by touch. The room stays difficult for strangers to picture, but the child needs a guide after dark. Safety has a cost here, paid in independence.

The family studies the room with you. The child remembers its landmarks better than any adult and points out a route no one had considered. The house becomes less mysterious, though the rest of the city remains open to anyone who can imagine it.

The child recognizes the room in the school photo and remembers who stood beside the camera. Your insistence on evidence keeps the business partner from being arrested on resemblance alone; the family still has to live with the fact that the photograph offered a stranger a map.

Your warning reaches the families before the police can name a suspect. Parents take photographs down, including the school portrait this child loved. The business partner remains free while the investigation continues, and the child asks whether being safe means being unseen.
The child recognizes the room in the school photo and remembers who stood beside the camera. The clue is useful, but it does not restore the family's feeling of safety.

choices.text: Campaign for shared rules and privacy protections
Help the family build a private, confusing refuge
Refuse to let fear decide where people may go

public.text: The city adopts rules against covert scans and unauthorized entry. They cannot stop a person from arriving anywhere, and the first prosecution fails when nobody can prove where a stranger began. But families no longer have to argue that privacy is a right only after an intrusion; consent becomes a public question rather than a private burden.

shelter.text: The family settles into its strange, carefully mapped rooms. The child knows the way by heart, but the family stops inviting people over; a home that cannot be found is also hard to share. Your plans become popular with those who can afford them, and a quiet new inequality takes shape between homes that can hide and homes that cannot.

open_city.text: You leave the locks untouched and start a neighborhood watch built on people checking in rather than shutting one another out. One neighbor refuses to join, remembering how quickly a watch becomes a list of strangers to suspect. You keep the door open anyway, knowing trust is not a lock: it can be offered, refused, and offered again.
